segments.tts: [slowly] [deep voice] Imagine a man who put Death in chains.
[knowingly] A man who fooled the gods not once… but twice.
[ominous] And who paid for it… forever, pushing a giant boulder up a hill.
[softly] Every time he nears the top, the boulder rolls back down. So he walks down… and begins again.
[mysterious] His name… Sisyphus.
[curious] So why did the gods punish him like this? [mysterious] And why, thousands of years later, did a thinker call him "happy"?
[warmly] The story begins on a narrow strip of land between two seas. Ephyra… known today as Corinth.
Its king was Sisyphus. They say he built up its ships and its trade, and made his city rich.
[wryly] But what truly made him famous was his mind. Homer calls him "the craftiest of men."
His neighbor, Autolycus, was a famous thief. So skilled, he could even change the color of the animals he stole. Each night, Sisyphus's herd grew a little smaller, but no one could prove a thing.
[mischievously] So Sisyphus carved tiny letters under his cattle's hooves. As they walked, they wrote a sentence in the earth: "Autolycus stole me."
[amused] The tracks led straight to the thief's barn. [darkly] But that same cleverness would one day make him a target of the gods.
[slowly] One day, watching the sky from the heights of his city, Sisyphus saw something.
[in awe] A giant eagle… carrying a young girl in its talons.
[mysterious] The eagle was Zeus in disguise. And the girl was Aegina, daughter of the river god Asopus.
The next day, Asopus went searching for his daughter. He wandered over mountains and plains… and at last, he came to Corinth.
[mischievously] Sisyphus smiled: "I know who took your daughter. But first… give my city a spring."
Asopus made fresh water burst from the rocks. And Sisyphus told him the secret.
[darkly] The city had its water. But Sisyphus had betrayed the king of the gods.
[ominous] [slowly] And Zeus… never forgot.
[slowly] Zeus sent his most terrible messenger to Sisyphus: Death himself… Thanatos.
[tense] Thanatos appeared at the palace door, carrying heavy chains.
[calmly] They say Sisyphus neither ran nor begged. He simply looked at the chains, curious.
[curious] "How do these go on? Could you show me?"
[wryly] Thanatos put the chains on his own wrists… and Sisyphus snapped the lock shut.
[slowly] [gravely] Death was in chains.
[in awe] No one in the world died anymore. Soldiers with fatal wounds got back on their feet, and not a single sacrifice could be made at the altars.
[wryly] Ares, the god of war, was furious. What was the point of a war where no one died?
[grimly] Ares freed Thanatos from his chains… and handed Sisyphus over to Death with his own hands.
[slowly] But before he died, Sisyphus had whispered something in the ear of his wife, Merope.
[whispers] "Don't bury my body. Hold no funeral for me. Make no offerings."
In the underworld, Sisyphus came before Persephone, queen of the dead.
[indignant] "My wife has disrespected me! No funeral, no offerings… Let me go up and punish her. I'll come right back."
[wryly] Persephone believed him.
[warmly] Sisyphus saw the sun again. The sea, the wine, his city… [wryly] And he never went back.
[warmly] He lived on for years. [darkly] Until Hermes, messenger of the gods, came and dragged him back by force.
[solemn] This time, the gods prepared a special punishment for Sisyphus.
[slowly] Deep in Tartarus, a steep hill. At the foot of the hill, a giant boulder.
His task was simple: get the boulder to the top.
[tense] He set his shoulder to the stone. He pushed. His feet slipped, his muscles shook… one step from the top, and then…
[sharply] The boulder broke free. And with a roar, it rolled all the way to the bottom.
[slowly] Sisyphus walked down. And began again.
[softly] The next day, too. And the day after that. A hundred years later… a thousand years later.
[darkly] Because the gods knew one thing: there is no more dreadful punishment than futile and hopeless labor.

[thoughtfully] More than two thousand years went by. In nineteen forty-two, with the world at war once again, a young writer named Albert Camus looked at this story with completely new eyes, in his essay, The Myth of Sisyphus.
[warmly] For Camus, there is a little Sisyphus in all of us. Every morning we get up, we work, we walk the same streets… and one day, we ask ourselves: "What is all this for?"
[slowly] The universe gives no answer. Camus calls this rift, between the human need for meaning and the silence of the world, "the absurd."
[thoughtfully] But what truly fascinated Camus was not the climb. It was the way back down, after the boulder falls, as Sisyphus descends with heavy but steady steps.
[softly] That return is like a breath. For Camus, it is the hour of consciousness. In that moment, Sisyphus is fully aware of his fate. And precisely because of that… he is stronger than his rock.
[warmly] The rock is his. His fate belongs to him. The gods gave him no meaning… but they could not crush him either.
[slowly] Camus ends his essay with these words:
[reverently] "The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart."
[softly] [slowly] "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."
[warmly] Maybe we all have a rock. A job, a responsibility, a dream… or simply, starting over every morning.
[softly] Maybe the point isn't getting the rock to the top. It's choosing who we become while we put our shoulder to it.
[softly] And you? What is your rock?
[warmly] Whatever your rock is, tell us in the comments. See you in the next story.
